Module 7 — Motion: Rotation, Animation, Audio · Lesson 7.7b

Animated Characters from glTF: Skins and Clips

Lessons 7.6 and 7.7 built every part of a character player and fed every part data the course wrote itself: a skeleton laid out joint by joint, a tube weighted by a formula, clips baked from functions. That proves the arithmetic and says nothing about content, because data you write yourself agrees with your code by construction. This lesson loads a character somebody else's tool wrote — a mannequin authored in Blender and exported by Blender's glTF exporter — and turns its node tree, its skin, its weights and its animation channels into the skeleton, skinned meshes and clips 7.6 and 7.7 already know how to play. The importer is five hundred lines of translation between index spaces and between curve types, and nearly every line exists because the file did something the engine's own data never had to: a node that is not a joint sitting above the hip, inverse binds that are data rather than something to derive, rotations written x, y, z, w, key frames joined by slerp, held by STEP or bent by cubic Hermite tangents, and — in the first export — twenty-five vertices the exporter quietly attached to a joint it invented. Four predictions Lesson 7.7 made about this lesson are tested and two of them are refused. The character plays within 40 µm of an independent double-precision evaluation of the specification's own formula.

Time
≈ 12 hours
Prereqs
6.6 — glTF 2.0 Loading, 7.5 — Slerp, and the Storage Swap, 7.6 — Skeletal Animation: The Skinning Math, 7.7 — Sampling and Blending Animations
Files
engine/include/engine/anim/import.hpp (new), engine/src/anim/import.cpp (new), engine/include/engine/gfx/gltf.hpp, engine/src/gfx/gltf.cpp, engine/include/engine/anim/skeleton.hpp, engine/src/anim/skeleton.cpp, engine/include/engine/anim/skin.hpp, engine/include/engine/engine.hpp, engine/CMakeLists.txt, demos/mannequin/main.cpp (new), demos/CMakeLists.txt, assets/mannequin.glb (new, binary), scratch/make_mannequin.py (new), scratch/verify_77b_blender.py (new), scratch/verify_77b_ex5.cpp (new), scratch/verify_77b.cpp (new), scratch/build_verify_77b.sh (new)
Milestone
The engine can play a character it did not build. 36 checks green, nine of them controls. Blender's mannequin — 21 nodes, 19 joints and one ancestor, 2,681 vertices in two primitives sharing one skin, a walk and a wave — imports in a quarter of a millisecond and plays within 39.5 µm of the specification's formula evaluated in double precision by code that shares nothing with the engine. The same motion exported as cubic splines imports to within 0.05°, and disagrees with the sampled export by 0.218° — which turns out to be Blender's disagreement with itself. Three checks in Lesson 7.6's files are corrected, because a real exporter and the specification showed they were wrong. Every later harness and the golden render (E917C06C) are unchanged.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to…

  • …read a glTF skin: say what skins.joints, inverseBindMatrices, JOINTS_n and WEIGHTS_n index, and compute a skinned vertex by hand from the specification's formula.
  • …build a parent-first skeleton from a node tree in any order, carrying the non-joint nodes above it, and say what an unsorted skeleton does to a character — precisely.
  • …treat a file's inverse bind matrices as data, apply the specification's default when they are absent, and measure how far a file's rest pose is from its bind pose.
  • …map per-vertex influences through three index spaces, keep four of any number, and hold a weighting to the specification's rules rather than to a guess.
  • …read rotations in the file's component order, and say what reading them in yours costs.
  • …convert LINEAR, STEP and CUBICSPLINE samplers into this engine's clips to a stated tolerance, and explain why the check must not sit at the midpoint.
  • …find, by measurement, the defects an exporter introduces without a warning — and tell them apart from your own.

1The problem: a character you did not build

Every skinned thing the engine has drawn so far, the engine built. Lesson 7.6's tube is six joints one unit apart up the y axis, weighted to its two nearest joints by a straight line; Lesson 7.7's clips are functions of time sampled thirty times a second and then reduced. Both lessons measured everything, and both measurements share a weakness that Module 8 named after it had cost several sections: data you write yourself agrees with your code by construction. The person who wrote the skeleton also wrote the code that reads it; any misunderstanding of what a joint's parent index means is in both, and the two agree.

A game does not ship characters written by its engine programmers. They come from a modelling tool, through an exporter somebody else wrote, in a format somebody else specified. Every one of those three has made decisions the engine never made for itself — about the order joints are written in, about where the character's transform lives, about how a rotation is written down, about what happens between two keys, about what to do with a vertex nobody weighted. An importer is the place those decisions are met, and the only way to meet them honestly is with a file the engine did not write.

So this lesson's character is not generated by a script of ours that writes glTF bytes, the way Lesson 6.6 wrote its cube. It is authored in Blender — a skin modifier grown over a stick figure, nineteen bones, Blender's own automatic weights, a walk and a wave keyed with Blender's default curves — and exported by Blender's glTF exporter, with its default settings. The authoring is a script too (scratch/make_mannequin.py), so anyone with Blender can rebuild the file byte for byte; but every decision the importer has to cope with is the exporter's. The file is assets/mannequin.glb, 193,000 bytes.

Lesson 7.7's last exercise sketched this lesson and made four predictions about it. Stating them here, where they can be wrong:

  1. the importer must topologically sort skins.joints and apply the same permutation to the tracks;
  2. a channel that targets a node which is not a joint is legal and must be dropped;
  3. the duration is not in the file, and is the maximum input time across the samplers;
  4. rotations arrive x, y, z, w, and a blind copy "turns into a 180° error about a diagonal axis" — and a real exporter's clips will contain sign flips.

The first and third hold. The second is wrong in a way that moves a character a metre (§3.3). The fourth is wrong twice: the error of a blind copy is not a fixed rotation at all (§7), and Blender's exporter produced no sign flips (§9.4). None of that could have been learned from a file the course wrote.

2Building intuition: a tree, and three lists that point into it

Lesson 6.6 described a glTF file as a scene rather than a shape: a tree of nodes, each with a local transform, some of them pointing at meshes. That lesson flattened the tree — it multiplied each mesh node's chain of transforms into one matrix and threw the chain away — and said so: "right for a static prop and wrong for anything with a skeleton". A skeleton is that tree. So the first thing to see is that nothing new has been added to the file to make it animated. Everything animated is a list that points into the tree:

  • A skin is a list of node indices, skins[k].joints. Being named there is what makes a node a joint; a node object "does not specify whether it is a joint" (spec §3.7.3.2). The position of a node in this list is its slot.
  • The inverse bind matrices are a second list, parallel to the first: slot r's matrix belongs to slot r's joint.
  • Each vertex's influences (JOINTS_0, WEIGHTS_0) point into the slots, not into the nodes.
  • Each animation channel points at a node and a property of it — translation, rotation or scale.

Three address books, in other words, each written in a different numbering, and none of them in ours. The engine's skeleton (7.6) has one numbering of its own, and it has a rule the file does not have to obey: a joint's parent must come before it. An importer's job is to build that one numbering and translate every other index into it, all in the same pass. Figure 1 is the mannequin's three orders, side by side.

Look at the first column before reading on. Blender wrote its node array children first — the head is node 0 and the Armature object, the root of everything, is node 20 — so every one of the nineteen joints has a parent with a larger index. A loader that built the skeleton by walking the node array would have every parent after its child. The second column is the skin's own list, and there Blender wrote parents first: hips, spine, chest, neck, head, then each arm and each leg from the top down. The third is what the importer builds, and it contains a joint the skin never named.

3What a glTF skin says

3.1 — The formula is Lesson 7.6's

The specification defines skinning in words (§3.7.3.3): "a transformation matrix is computed for each joint. Then, the per-vertex transformation matrices are computed as weighted linear sums of the joint transformation matrices", and the inverse bind matrices "MUST be applied before the base node transforms". Written down:

\[ \mathbf{v}' \;=\; \sum_i w_i\, \big(G_{j_i}\, B_{j_i}\big)\, \mathbf{v} \] v' = sum over i of w_i * (G[j_i] * B[j_i]) * v

where Gj is joint j's global transform — its local transform multiplied by every ancestor's, up to the root of the scene — and Bj is its inverse bind matrix. That is Lesson 7.6's palette entry exactly: palette[j] = model_from_joint[j] * joint_from_model[j], "where the joint is now" times "where it was when the mesh was bound to it". The only question is what "model space" means for a file, and the answer falls out of the next two sentences of the specification.

3.2 — The mesh node's own transform is ignored

A skinned mesh in glTF hangs from a node like any other mesh, and that node has a transform. The specification (§3.7.3.2) is explicit about what happens to it: "Only the joint transforms are applied to the skinned mesh; the transform of the skinned mesh node MUST be ignored." The reason is the formula above. A skinned vertex's position is decided entirely by the joints it is bound to — Gj already carries it all the way to the scene's root — so there is nothing left for the mesh node to do. A viewer that applied the node's transform as well would move the character twice.

3.3 — The common root, and the nodes above it

Here is the sentence prediction (2) overlooked. Gj is a global transform, and a global transform includes every ancestor, whether it is a joint or not: "The global transformation matrix of a node is the product of the global transformation matrix of its parent node and its own local transformation matrix" (§3.5.3). The specification requires that each skin's joints "MUST have a common parent node (direct or indirect) called common root, which may or may not be a joint node itself" — and in Blender's file it is not: the hip's parent is the Armature object, node 20, which no skin names. Converters from other tools routinely hang a 0.01 scale or a quarter turn about x on exactly that node.

So the importer does not drop the nodes above the joints. It carries them into the skeleton as joints — joints no vertex is weighted to, whose only job is to be in every joint's chain. With every ancestor carried, the skeleton's roots are the scene's roots, and "model space" in the engine is exactly the file's scene space. A channel that animates the Armature node — Blender will export one if the object itself is keyed — then animates a joint like any other, which is what the file meant.

3.4 — The specification's own example, with numbers

The specification illustrates the rule with a five-node example and a sentence: "the translation of node_0 and the scale of node_1 are applied while the translation of node_3 and rotation of node_4 are ignored". It gives no mesh and no numbers. The harness completes it into a file (§B), and Figure 2 is the result.

Worked example. Joint A is node_1, under node_0; joint B is node_2, one unit along A's x.

GA = T(0,1,0) · S(0.5)               BA = GA−1 = S(2) · T(0,−1,0)
GB = T(0,1,0) · S(0.5) · T(1,0,0)   BB = GB−1 = S(2) · T(−0.5,−1,0)
v0 = (0, 1, 0), weighted 1 to A:  GABAv0 = I · v0 = (0, 1, 0)

At rest every palette matrix is the identity and the triangle is exactly where the file put it. Now the two wrong answers. An importer that applied the mesh node's transform, T(1,0,0) · Ry(180°), sends v0 to (1, 1, 0) — the rotation fixes a point on the y axis and the translation moves it a metre. An importer that dropped the non-joint node_0 computes GA = S(0.5), so the palette entry is S(0.5) · S(2) · T(0,−1,0) = T(0,−1,0), and v0 lands at (0, 0, 0) — a metre under the floor, from a rule that sounded like tidiness.

node_1 turns 90° about z over one second:
BBv1 = S(2)·((0.5,1,0) − (0.5,1,0)) = (0,0,0)    v1 is B's origin
t = 1:   T(0,1,0)·S(0.5)·Rz(90°)·(1,0,0) = T(0,1,0)·(0,0.5,0) = (0, 1.5, 0)
t = 0.5: (0.5 cos 45°, 1 + 0.5 sin 45°) = (0.35355, 1.35355, 0)

The engine's answers, from the harness:

  rest: v0 (0.000, 1.000, 0.000)  v1 (0.500, 1.000, 0.000)
  control, mesh node applied: v0 -> (1.000, 1.000, 0.000)
  control, node_0 dropped: v0 -> (0.000, 0.000, 0.000)
  t=1    v1 (0.00000, 1.50000)   predicted (0, 1.5)
  t=0.5  v1 (0.35355, 1.35355)   predicted (0.35355, 1.35355)
  t=0.25 v1 (0.46183, 1.19160)   spec (0.46194, 1.19134)

Two things in that transcript are worth a sentence now and a section later. The quarter-second line is not exact: the specification says a rotation between two keys is slerped, our sampler nlerps, and the importer inserted two keys so that the difference stays under 0.05° — at this joint's half-metre lever, 0.28 mm (§8.2). And the t=1 line needed the importer to be told the clip does not loop. glTF has no loop flag; with the importer's default the time 1 s wraps to 0 and v1 is back at rest (§9.2).

4The skeleton: every node above the joints, parent first

4.1 — Which nodes

The joints, and every node on the path from each joint up to its scene root. The walk up is the parent pointer the parser records for every node (gltf_node_desc::parent), bounded by the node count so that a malformed file cannot make it loop — cgltf's validator already refuses a cycle, and the bound costs nothing.

4.2 — Which order: a sort that moves nothing it does not have to

Lesson 7.6 put one requirement on a skeleton — joints[i].parent < i — so that compose_pose could be a single loop with no sorting, and left the sort to "whoever imports a rig", paid once. Any topological order satisfies it. The importer uses a particular one: 

for each joint, in the skin's order:
    walk up from it until a node already placed (or the root),
    and place that chain top-down.

Every node is placed after its parent, because a chain is placed from the top. Ancestors land immediately before their first descendant. And a skin that was already parent-first comes out in exactly its own order, because each joint's parent was placed by the time the joint is reached. That last property is the reason for choosing this sort over a textbook one: it makes a number meaningful. rig_import_report::resorted counts the skin joints whose rank among the skin's joints changed, and on a file that needed no sorting it reads zero — so a non-zero value means the exporter really did write children first, rather than that the sort shuffled things for its own reasons. The cost is O(joints × depth) with a small constant; the mannequin's depth is 8.

The mannequin, and a four-joint chain the harness writes tip first:

  skin joints 19; parents AFTER child in node order: 19
  import ok: 20 joints = 19 skin + 1 ancestor
  file-order breaks 0, resorted 0
  root joint 'Armature', identity IBMs no
  ...
  file-order breaks 3, resorted 4, identity IBMs yes
  our order: root lower upper tip

On Blender's file the sort does nothing at all. That is the most dangerous kind of result a test can give: an importer that forgot to sort would pass every test run against Blender's output and fail on the first file from a tool that writes children first. The hand-written chain is there so that the sort is tested on a file that needs it — three of its four joints come before their parents in the skin, and after the sort all four have moved.

4.3 — What the sort prevents, and a correction to Lesson 7.6

Lesson 7.6's skeleton.hpp described what an out-of-order joint does, and the description was vivid: the parent's matrix "has not been written yet when the child reads it, so the child composes against last frame's value — which looks like a one-frame lag that grows with depth". Build a skeleton in a file's child-first order and compose it twice, with a joint turned between the two, and the harness reports: 

  control, file order: out_of_order 3; tip y 1.000, then 1.000
  [PASS] C.5 unsorted, the tip is a root at y = 1 on BOTH frames

No lag. The tip sits at y = 1 — its own one-unit offset, measured from the model's origin — on both frames, and the turn of its grandparent never reaches it. The comment described what an unguarded loop would do. compose_pose has a guard: a parent index at or after the child's is treated as no parent at all, so the child composes as a root. The chain is cut, not delayed, and it is cut on every frame. Figure 3 is the mannequin built in the node array's order, where nineteen of twenty joints are out of order: every limb is composed as a root at its local offset from the origin, and the character is a pile of parts at its own feet.

The comment is corrected in this lesson's skeleton.hpp and skeleton.cpp, with the measurement cited. It is the kind of error that survives because it is plausible and nothing ever exercises it: 7.6's skeletons were always built in order, so the guard's behaviour was never observed until a file arrived that was not.

5Inverse binds are data

5.1 — Derived in 7.6, primary in a file

Lesson 7.6 derived the inverse bind matrices from the bind pose — one forward pass, parent before child, no general inverse anywhere — and then made an argument for never storing them anywhere else: "a field an editor could hand-write would be a field that can disagree with the bind pose beside it". For a skeleton the engine authors, that stands. A file is a skeleton somebody else authored, and in glTF the argument runs the other way. The node transforms are simply the pose the file was saved in — the rest pose if the artist exported at rest, a frame of the walk if they did not — while the inverse bind matrices are the bind, stated once and authoritatively. When the two disagree, the matrices are right and the nodes are merely where the character happens to be standing.

So import_rig bakes every joint's inverse bind the 7.6 way and then overwrites the skin's joints with the file's matrices. The ancestors keep their baked values: no vertex is weighted to them, and baking makes their skinning matrix the identity at rest, which keeps the one number below about the file rather than about joints the file never bound. skeleton.hpp's comment that the array is "written by bake_inverse_binds and by nothing else" is amended in this lesson to say why that stopped being true.

5.2 — Absent is not missing

A skin may omit its inverseBindMatrices accessor, and the obvious response — compute them from the rest pose, the way 7.6 would — is wrong. The specification (§5.28.1): "When undefined, each matrix is a 4x4 identity matrix." A file without inverse binds is saying that its mesh is already in each joint's space, not that it forgot. The harness's chain has no accessor, and a vertex at the origin weighted to the tip: 

  identity IBMs: v0 at y = 3.000 (the tip is at 3)
  [PASS] C.3 absent IBMs are the identity, not baked
  control, IBMs baked from rest: v0 at y = 0.000
  [PASS] C.4 control: baking moves it to the origin

With the identity, a vertex at the tip's origin rides the tip, three units up. Baked from the rest pose, the same vertex is carried to the tip's space and back and lands at the model's origin — a character whose every vertex has collapsed onto the point it was modelled around.

5.3 — One number for how the file was saved

7.6's skeleton_report::worst_bind_residual poses a skeleton at its own rest pose and measures how far each palette matrix is from the identity. On a skeleton the engine baked, it measures float error through the chain. On an imported one it answers a different question with the same arithmetic, because the two factors now come from two different places in the file: how far the pose the file was saved in is from the pose it was bound in. It is reported as bind_vs_rest: 

  bind vs rest 2.894e-06, depth 8, nonuniform binds 0

Blender's exporter writes both from the rest pose, and they agree to float noise. A file saved mid-walk would report the walk's angles here — not an error, and not something to fix: the importer uses the matrices either way, and the number tells you the character will not stand in its bind pose when no clip is playing.

5.4 — A check that fired on a healthy rig

The same line says nonuniform binds 0, and the first run said 12. Lesson 7.6 counted a joint as non-uniformly scaled when its three scale components were not exactly equal — the condition under which the engine's normal rule is wrong by 22.6° at a 1.5:1 stretch. Blender's exporter writes rest scales like (1.0000009, 0.9999996, 1.0000086): float noise from decomposing a matrix, and twelve of twenty joints tripped the exact test. A check that fires on a healthy file teaches its reader to ignore it, which is worse than no check.

The fix is a tolerance, chosen from two measurements rather than one. The noise is a relative spread of 8.94 × 10−6; the normal error a stretch of that size causes, measured on a 45° normal, is 5.1 × 10−4 degrees. The new k_uniform_scale_tolerance is 10−4 — eleven times the noise, where the normal error would be 5.7 × 10−3 degrees, and five thousand times smaller than the 1.5:1 stretch 7.6 worried about, which the control confirms is still counted: 

  Blender's rest scales: worst relative spread 8.94e-06
  nonuniform_binds reports 0 of 20 joints
  [PASS] I.1 float noise in a rest scale is not a non-uniform bind
  [PASS] I.2 control: a 1.5:1 stretch is still counted
  normal error: 5.13e-04 deg at Blender's spread, 5.73e-03 at 1e-4

6Influences: three index spaces, four slots

6.1 — One vertex, followed

JOINTS_0 holds, per vertex, four indices "of the joints from the corresponding skin.joints array" (§3.7.3.3) — slots, not nodes. The importer builds one table, slot → joint, when it builds the skeleton, and every vertex goes through it. Figure 4 follows vertex 28 of the body, at the top of the legs, through all three spaces.

Three places where an importer mixes up spaces, and each has a signature. Reading the slot as a node index animates each vertex by a joint with an unrelated number — the body shreds. Reading it as our joint index without the table animates it by the joint one place away, because our skeleton has the Armature at index 0 and every skin joint shifted by one — the whole character moves as if every bone's neighbour were driving it. And forgetting to renumber the inverse binds along with the joints pairs each joint with its neighbour's bind, which looks like both.

6.2 — More than four

Lesson 7.6 fixed four influences per vertex, because four indices and four weights are one GPU register each. glTF allows any number, in sets: "When any of the vertices are influenced by more than four joints, the additional joint and weight information are stored in subsequent sets", JOINTS_1 with WEIGHTS_1 and so on. The parser reads every set that pairs up; the importer keeps the four largest weights and renormalises, which 7.6 named as the standard step, and reports what it threw away — because the error of dropping a weight w is at most w times the distance between where that joint and the others would put the vertex, so the dropped weight is the number that bounds the damage.

Blender's default export already keeps four ("Bone influences: 4"), so the mannequin has nothing to drop. The harness builds a triangle with six influences in two sets — 0.3, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1 and 0.15, 0.1: 

  six influences: sets 2, truncated 3, worst dropped 0.10
  kept joints j0 j1 j2 j4, weights 0.3750 0.2500 0.1875 0.1875

Worked example. Sorted largest first: 0.3 (j0), 0.2 (j1), 0.15 (j2), 0.15 (j4), 0.1 (j3), 0.1 (j5). Two weights tie at 0.15; the sort is stable_sort, so j2 keeps its place ahead of j4 because it came first in the file, and the result does not depend on which standard library compiled it. Keep four; the kept sum is 0.8; divide:

0.3/0.8 = 0.375   0.2/0.8 = 0.25   0.15/0.8 = 0.1875   0.15/0.8 = 0.1875

6.3 — What a weight sum is allowed to miss by

Lesson 7.6's skin.hpp set the tolerance on a weight sum at 0.02 and argued for it: weights stored as normalised bytes, 1/255 a step, "can miss by up to 4/255 = 0.0157 before anyone has done anything wrong". Reading the specification for this lesson refuted the premise. For normalised unsigned bytes and shorts, "their linear sum before normalization MUST be 255 or 65535 respectively" — an exporter quantises and then fixes the sum, so a conforming file misses by nothing at all. A byte-weighted vertex one step short is somebody's mistake, and the specification says what it costs: the error "would get multiplied by the joint position". A sum of 254/255 pulls a vertex 1/255 of the way toward the model's origin — 7 mm at the top of a 1.8 m character — and 0.02 let it through without a word.

So k_weight_tolerance is now 10−5, placed between the two things a sum can be off by: above float noise (the specification's validator allows 2 × 10−7 per non-zero weight, and Blender's worst is 8.57 × 10−8) and below the smallest step a quantised file can miss by, 1/65535 = 1.5 × 10−5. 

  worst weight sum error in the file 8.57e-08
  [PASS] D.1 Blender's weights sum to 1 within 2e-7 x 4
  byte weights 255/255 and 254/255: unnormalised 1
  [PASS] I.3 a quantised sum one step short is reported

6.4 — What the character's vertices kept

The histogram at the bottom of Figure 4 is the whole mannequin: 48.5% of its vertices follow a single joint, 40.8% blend two, 7.4% three and 3.2% four. That is what Blender's automatic weights produce on a body made of tubes — most of the surface belongs to one bone, and blending happens in bands around the joints. It is also the argument for the four-influence limit, measured rather than assumed: on this content nothing needed a fifth.

6.5 — A step that renumbers vertices

One more thing moves influences, and it is not in the importer. If a primitive has no normals, the parser generates flat ones, and flat normals split vertices: with_normals writes one vertex per triangle corner (Lesson 3.6). Every array it knows about is rebuilt; the influence arrays are the parser's own, so the parser follows the split itself, taking new vertex k's influences from old vertex indices[k]. Forget it and each corner inherits the influences of whichever vertex used to have its number, and the mesh deforms like shredded paper. Blender always writes normals, so this path never runs on the mannequin; every hand-written file in the harness omits them, so it runs on all of those.

7Rotations arrive x, y, z, w

"rotation is a unit quaternion value, XYZW, in the local coordinate system, where W is the scalar" (§3.5.3). This engine stores quat{w, v}, scalar first (conventions: quat). The swizzle is one line, and it lives in one function, quat_from_xyzw in gltf.hpp, which both readers of a file rotation call — the parser for node rotations and the importer for animation keys — so there is exactly one place for it to be wrong.

7.1 — What a blind copy costs

Lesson 7.7's prediction was that copying the four floats straight into a quat "turns into a 180° error about a diagonal axis". Work two cases by hand before measuring. A blind copy puts the file's (x, y, z, w) into (w, x, y, z):

identity  file (0, 0, 0, 1) → w = 0, v = (0, 0, 1)   = 180° about z
(½, ½, ½, ½) file (½, ½, ½, ½) → w = ½, v = (½, ½, ½) = itself: 0° of error

The identity becomes a half turn — about z, not a diagonal. And a quaternion whose four components are equal is its own shift, so its error is zero. One misreading, two keys, 180° and 0°: the error is not a fixed rotation.

That is not a coincidence of two cases, and the reason is short. Moving four components one place along is a cyclic permutation of four things, which is an odd permutation — three swaps — and as a linear map on ℝ4 it has determinant −1. Multiplying every quaternion by one fixed unit quaternion, on either side, is a rotation of ℝ4, with determinant +1. So no fixed rotation composed with the right one reproduces the blind copy; the error depends on the key. Over every rotation key in Blender's file: 

  748 rotation keys: error min 110.9, median 168.5, max 180.0 deg
  identity -> 180.0 deg about (0, 0, 1)
  (1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2) -> error 0.0 deg

Never small on this content — the smallest error on any key is 111° — and never the same twice, which is why no "fix-up rotation" applied afterwards can hide it. Figure 5 is the result. The first joint in the chain is the Armature node, whose rotation is the identity, so the whole character is turned 180° about z before anything else goes wrong: it hangs upside down, a metre under the floor, with every limb folded by its own unrelated error.

Lesson 7.7's exercise is corrected to match. And one more place a file's rotation is decoded: a rotation may be stored as normalised signed bytes or shorts, which the specification decodes as max(c / 127, −1). cgltf 1.15 divides without the max, so the one value with no positive twin, −128, reads as −1.0079. A rotation key is renormalised on import anyway, so it changes no picture; the parser clamps it because a decode that disagrees with the specification is a bug report waiting for the asset that finds it.

8Curves: the file's three, and our one

A glTF sampler is a list of key times and a list of values, and an interpolation mode that says what happens between keys (Appendix C): LINEAR — which "when targeting a rotation" means spherical linear interpolation, slerp — STEP, which holds each key until the next, and CUBICSPLINE, a Hermite curve with a tangent on each side of every key. Lesson 7.7's sampler has one rule per field and no modes at all: lerp for position and scale, nlerp for rotation. Only LINEAR on a position or a scale is already ours.

Rather than teach the sampler three more modes — and every future consumer of a clip with it — the importer converts. Each interval between two file keys is split into the fewest equal pieces for which our interpolation of the file's curve stays within a tolerance of the file's curve itself, and the interior keys are written at the file curve's exact values. The error is measured with the sampler's own rule, which is Lesson 7.7's reducer's principle arriving from the other side.

The tolerance is a tenth of the reducer's: 0.1 mm, 0.05° and 10−4 of scale, against reduce's 1 mm, 0.5° and 10−3. The two errors can add — the reducer judges the importer's curve, not the file's — and the first argument for a tenth was an error budget split between them. Exercise 5 measured it and the argument changed. Importing Blender's cubic walk at 0.005°, 0.05° and 0.25° and then reducing at 0.5° ends 0.501°, 0.512° and 0.513° from an exact import: the errors barely add. What moves is the key count after reduction — 258, 276, 329 — because a looser import leaves wiggles the reducer then has to follow. A strict import costs keys before the reducer and saves them after it, and a tenth is where the saving had mostly arrived.

8.1 — Measured where the error is, not at the midpoint

Before splitting anything the importer has to measure the difference between the file's curve and ours on an interval, and the obvious place to measure is the middle. For the most common case — a LINEAR rotation — the middle is exactly the place where there is nothing to see.

Put the two keys on the unit sphere of quaternions, an arc Ω apart. Slerp walks the arc at constant speed: at parameter u it is uΩ along. Nlerp walks the straight chord and pushes the result back onto the sphere, and the angle it has covered is the angle of that chord point seen from the centre:

\[ \varphi_{\text{nlerp}}(u) = \operatorname{atan2}\!\big(u \sin\Omega,\; (1-u) + u\cos\Omega\big), \qquad \varphi_{\text{slerp}}(u) = u\,\Omega \] phi_nlerp(u) = atan2(u sin W, (1 - u) + u cos W); phi_slerp(u) = u W

Both paths lie on the same great circle; only the schedule differs. At u = ½ the chord point is the midpoint of the chord, which lies on the bisector of the arc, so both are at Ω/2 exactly — the two agree at the one place a single probe would look. The lag peaks near a fifth and four fifths of the way.

Worked example. A 90° rotation between two keys is a sphere arc of Ω = 45° (a quaternion carries the half angle). At u = ¼:

φ_nlerp = atan2(0.25 · sin 45°, 0.75 + 0.25 · cos 45°)
        = atan2(0.17678, 0.92678) = 10.799°
φ_slerp = 0.25 · 45° = 11.250°
lag    = 0.451° on the sphere = 0.902° of rotation
at u = ½: atan2(0.35355, 0.85355) = 22.500° = ½ · 45°  — zero

Say which degrees

Every number on this page is an angle of rotation. Lesson 7.5's table — "0.13 degrees at a 30-degree arc, 4.07 at 90" — is in sphere degrees, the quaternion's half-angle: a 30° sphere arc is a 60° rotation, and the harness's 0.2675° of rotation lag at 60° is its 0.134°. The two conventions differ by exactly a factor of two in both columns, which is precisely the kind of difference that survives review.

So the importer measures at seven probes inside every piece — ⅛, ²⁄₈, … ⅞ — which straddle both peaks. The harness keeps the midpoint as a control: it must see nothing, at every arc. Figure 6 is the lag and the number of pieces it takes to stay within 0.05°. 

  arc   nlerp lag (at u)    at u=.5   pieces  residual
   15.5   0.0046 deg (0.786)  8.5e-07     1
   30.0   0.0331 deg (0.788)  1.7e-06     1
   60.0   0.2675 deg (0.214)  0.0e+00     2
   90.0   0.9188 deg (0.217)  3.4e-06     3
  120.0   2.2340 deg (0.223)  3.4e-06     4
  150.0   4.5140 deg (0.771)  0.0e+00     5
  179.0   8.0010 deg (0.762)  6.8e-06     6
  split keys 15, worst residual 0.0323 deg (limit 0.05)
  [PASS] E.1 every arc is fitted within 0.05 degrees
  [PASS] E.2 control: at the midpoint nlerp and slerp agree

And on Blender's file? The exporter sampled every frame at 30 Hz, so adjacent keys are never more than 17.6° apart (the wave's arm, rising), where the lag is 0.0065° — an eighth of the tolerance. Every one of the mannequin's intervals is accepted with one piece: 929 keys in and 929 out, worst residual 0.0065°. The machinery exists for files that were not sampled: hand-keyed LINEAR curves with keys far apart, which is exactly the kind of file a runtime format's size budget encourages.

8.2 — STEP: one float before the next key

A STEP sampler's value is "vt = vk" for the whole interval, and then jumps. Our sampler has no step mode, and does not need one. Two keys holding the same value one representable time apart are a step, to within the one float between them: the importer writes each key, and when the next key's value differs, a copy of this one at nextafter(tk+1, −∞). Figure 7 is the harness's case — a translation keyed 0, 1, 2 at 0, ½ and 1 s. 

  STEP 0,1,2 at 0, .5, 1 s: keys 5 (2 of them held)
  x(.25) 0.000   x(.5 - 1 ulp) 0.000   x(.5) 1.000
  [PASS] E.3 a STEP holds to the float before its next key
  control, keys copied as-is: x(.25) 0.500
  [PASS] E.4 control: copied, a STEP becomes a ramp

Blender's file has a great deal of STEP in it, and none of it needs a held key. The exporter writes every property of every bone — translation, rotation and scale for nineteen bones, 57 channels per animation — and writes the ones that never change as a two-key STEP sampler holding one value. 95 of the file's 114 channels are that. Equal values need no hold, so the importer adds nothing; Lesson 7.7's reducer then deletes them entirely (§9.5).

8.3 — CUBICSPLINE, and the td nobody reads

Each key of a cubic sampler carries three values — an in-tangent a, the value v and an out-tangent b — and the curve on an interval of length td = tk+1 − tk is the Hermite cubic (§C.5):

\[ v(u) = (2u^3 - 3u^2 + 1)\,v_k + t_d\,(u^3 - 2u^2 + u)\,b_k + (-2u^3 + 3u^2)\,v_{k+1} + t_d\,(u^3 - u^2)\,a_{k+1} \] v(u) = (2u^3 - 3u^2 + 1) v_k + t_d (u^3 - 2u^2 + u) b_k + (-2u^3 + 3u^2) v_(k+1) + t_d (u^3 - u^2) a_(k+1)

The four polynomials are the standard Hermite basis: the first and third blend the two values, the second and fourth add the slopes, and each vanishes where the others need it to. The factor td is the part to read twice. The tangents in the file are rates per second; the basis runs over u, which goes from 0 to 1 across the interval whatever its length. A slope per second times seconds per unit of u is a slope per unit of u, and td is that conversion.

Worked example. A scalar from 0 to 1 over td = 0.5 s, leaving at slope 2 per second and arriving flat (bk = 2, ak+1 = 0). At u = ½ the basis is 0.5, 0.125, 0.5, −0.125:

with t_d:    0.5·0 + 0.5·0.125·2 + 0.5·1 + 0.5·(−0.125)·0 = 0.625
without t_d: 0.5·0 +    0.125·2 + 0.5·1                  = 0.750

Leaving out td multiplies every tangent by 1/td: twice as steep here, and on the intervals animators actually key — a few frames — far worse.

For a rotation the specification evaluates the Hermite on the four raw components and then requires that "the interpolated quaternion MUST be normalized". It does not pick the nearer sign first — it tells exporters instead to avoid writing a key that is the negation of the next — and the importer follows the formula exactly, because the point of a reference curve is that it is the specification's.

Blender writes cubic splines when "Always Sample Animations" is off: each Bezier curve an animator keyed arrives as its keys and their tangents. The authoring script exports the same scene that way as well, and the importer converts it: 

  Blender, sampling off: 39 cubic channels, 332 keys in
  -> 1227 keys out (895 split), worst 0.0500 deg / 9.66e-05 m
  [PASS] E.5 Blender's CUBICSPLINE fitted within tolerance
  control, tangents without t_d: curve off by 40.25 deg
  [PASS] E.6 control: forgetting t_d moves the curve by degrees

Figure 8 is one of those channels, the left thigh during the walk. Blender's keys are four frames apart, td = 0.133 s, so a forgotten td makes every tangent 7.5 times too steep, and the curve overshoots between every pair of keys by as much as 40°. (The first draft of the importer's own comment on this said the opposite — that a forgotten td "flattens" a short curve. The plot of the mistake is what corrected it: only an interval longer than a second comes out flatter.)

Nine keys became 61 on that channel, and 332 became 1,227 across the file: cubic curves bend everywhere, and 0.05° is a tight budget for a straight line to follow a bend. That is the price of the tolerance being a tenth of the reducer's, and it is paid back the moment the reducer runs — the reducer exists precisely to merge keys a straight line can already reach.

8.4 — Two exports of one motion

The authoring script exports the same walk twice: sampled at every frame (the default), and as curves. Same armature, same keys, same Bezier handles — two files that describe one motion. Import both, sample both, and compare every joint, 240 times across the second: 

  walk, sampled vs curves: worst joint 0.916 deg (on frames 0.218)
  the same, from the files alone (no importer): 0.218 deg
  [PASS] E.7 the two exports differ, and by the exporter's amount

The prediction written before the run was that the two would agree on the frames, where the sampled export stores Blender's own evaluation, to within the importer's 0.05°. They do not: 0.218° on the frames and 0.916° between them. Before blaming Blender, the harness asks whose disagreement it is by removing the importer altogether: evaluate the curves file with the specification's formula at each frame time and compare with the sampled file's key there. 0.218°, to three decimals. The two files disagree with each other by exactly the amount the imports do, so the import adds nothing measurable; the difference is in the files. Figure 9 shows it over time.

So what is Blender doing? The explanation first written here was about Bezier handles: a Blender curve is a Bezier curve in (frame, value) with two-dimensional handles, and it equals a Hermite curve only when every handle sits a third of the way along its interval in time. The walk is keyed at frames 0, 4, 8, 11, 15… — intervals of four and three frames — and the guess was that Blender's automatic handles on a key between unequal intervals are not at a third of either. Asking Blender (scratch/verify_77b_blender.py) refused it: every handle is at 0.333 of its interval, 1.333 frames of a four-frame gap and 1.000 of a three. A slope-only conversion of those handles is exact.

The real mechanism is one line further into the exporter. To carry a tangent from Blender's bone space into the node space glTF wants, the exporter turns it into a control point — the key's value plus one frame of slope — transforms that point the same way it transforms a key, and subtracts the transformed key; its own comment says this "only works for locally linear transformation" and that its author is "not sure that linearity is never broken with quaternions and their normalization". It is broken. A rotation is transformed by transform_rotation (io_scene_gltf2/blender/com/gltf2_blender_math.py), whose first line is rotation.normalize(), and a key plus a slope is not a unit quaternion. Normalising it bends the tangent, by an amount that grows with the slope — so the error appears where a joint turns fastest. The same script evaluates Blender's own curve against two Hermites built from the same keys: 

TAN shin.R frame 1: linear tangents 0.0000 deg, exporter's 0.1045 deg
TAN shin.R frame 2: linear tangents 0.0000 deg, exporter's 0.2182 deg
TAN shin.R frame 3: linear tangents 0.0000 deg, exporter's 0.1558 deg
TAN worst over four bones, every tenth of a frame: linear 0.0000, exporter 0.2211

With the true tangents the Hermite is Blender's curve, to four decimals. With the exporter's normalised ones it misses by 0.1045°, 0.2182° and 0.1558° on frames 1 to 3 of the right shin's bend — and the two files, compared directly, disagree there by 0.103°, 0.216° and 0.157°. That is the whole of the disagreement: the knee sweeping 55° in four frames, a tangent large enough for a normalisation to notice.

Neither the importer nor the specification is at fault, and neither file is wrong in a way a validator would catch. The lesson is about instruments, twice. The first draft of this check would have reported an importer bug, and the second arm — the files alone — moved the blame to the exporter. The first explanation of the exporter's error was then wrong too, and it took asking the tool that made the file, rather than reasoning about it, to find the line that was. Which export should a game ship? The sampled one is Blender's own evaluation of its curves; the cubic one is smaller in the file, larger once imported, and a fifth of a degree off where joints move fast.

9A clip from an animation

With the curves converted, a glTF animation becomes one anim::clip: a track per joint, parallel to the skeleton — so the permutation the sort produced is applied to the tracks by construction, which was 7.7's first prediction — and three channels per track. What the file does not say, the importer has to decide, and there are four decisions.

9.1 — The duration is not in the file

glTF has no duration. The specification says the inputs "are relative to t = 0, defined as the beginning of the parent animations entry" and that outside a sampler's range "output MUST be clamped to the nearest end" — so an animation's natural length is the last input of any of its samplers, and that is what the importer uses. Lesson 7.7 argued that a clip's duration should be authored, because the last key of a walk sampled at 30 Hz can land a frame short of the cycle; here the argument arrives from the other side, and Blender answers it. The exporter writes the closing frame — frame 30 of a 30-frame walk, frame 60 of the wave — whose pose repeats the opening one, so the last input is the cycle's length. 7.7's instrument confirms it: 

  clip walk  1.000 s  keys 520  seam 9.84e-07 deg
  clip wave  2.000 s  keys 409  seam 7.76e-07 deg

9.2 — Looping is the importer's choice, and the specification clamps

glTF "doesn't define any runtime behavior, such as: order of playing, auto-start, loops" (§3.11), so import_settings::loops decides, and defaults to true because the clips this engine plays are cycles. That decision has a consequence at the end of the clip that twice looked like a bug in this lesson. Past the last key the specification clamps; a looping clip wraps. Sampled at exactly t = 1 s, §3.4's one-second turn returned to rest until the harness imported it with loops = false. And the first draft of the end-to-end check (§13) sampled at 1.013 s, compared the wrapped pose with the specification's clamped one, and reported an 11.7 mm "error" that was the walk's motion over thirteen milliseconds. Neither was wrong; they were two definitions of what comes after the end.

9.3 — What stays still stays where the file put it

A channel the animation does not animate is left empty in the track, and 7.7's sampler fills an empty channel with the joint's local_bind. For an imported rig that is the node's own transform — which is exactly what the specification requires: "Non-animated properties MUST keep their values during animation" (§3.11). This is the second reason §5 left local_bind holding the node's transform rather than the bind pose the inverse matrices describe: it is the rest value of every channel no clip touches.

9.4 — Sign flips: none, on this content

Lesson 7.7's prediction was that a real exporter's clips would contain adjacent rotation keys on opposite halves of the sphere, and that finding some would prove the importer read the file. canonicalise_rotations runs on every imported clip and counts them: 

  sign flips 0, frozen vertices 0

Zero. That is not the exporter canonicalising, as far as this file can tell; it is the content. A sign flip needs a rotation that passes the half-turn from rest, where w changes sign — and the mannequin's keys were authored as Euler angles under 180° and never go near one. The prediction was a claim about exporters, and the measurement can only speak for this file: the count is zero because nothing here could have produced one, which is a reason to keep the counter rather than a reason to remove it.

9.5 — 7.7's reducer, on real content

An imported clip is exactly as dense as the file, and the file wrote everything — every property of every bone, sampled or held. Lesson 7.7's reduce exists for this, and it takes the importer's clips unchanged: 

  walk  keys  520 -> 195 (-325), channels 57 -> 14
          9980 B ->  3828 B, worst playback 0.498 deg
  wave  keys  409 -> 103 (-306), channels 57 ->  5
          7876 B ->  2060 B, worst playback 0.494 deg

Forty-three of the walk's 57 channels and 52 of the wave's are Blender's constant STEP channels, and the reducer deletes them outright: each one holds a single value that equals the node's rest transform, and 7.7's third stage removes a channel whose one value is the bind value, because the sampler would reproduce it anyway. What is left is the motion — the walk's thirteen turning joints and the hip's bob — within the reducer's half degree. The importer did not reduce by default, and that is deliberate: reduction is lossy and budgeted, and whether to spend the budget is the caller's decision. The demo plays either with R.

10The first export: a joint nobody animates

The first time the importer ran on the mannequin, its joint table had twenty skin joints, not nineteen. The twentieth was called neutral_bone. It is not in the armature the script builds; it is a child of the Armature node with no animation channel, and twenty-five vertices were weighted to it — all of them at the tip of the nose.

Blender's automatic weights solve a heat-diffusion problem over the surface from each bone, and on the thin protrusion of the nose the solution for every bone fell below the exporter's threshold. The exporter's response is in its source (io_scene_gltf2/blender/exp/primitive_extract.py): a vertex with no influence above 0.0001 is given full weight on "a joint that will be created later", and tree.py creates it — neutral_bone, parented to the armature, appended to the skin. The file is valid. Every weight sums to one. Nothing warns. And the nose tip is rigidly attached to a joint that never moves, so when the head turns, the tip stays behind.

A check for "a joint named neutral_bone" would find this one exporter's convention and nothing else. The importer measures the general condition instead: frozen_vertices counts the vertices no clip in the file can move — every joint they are weighted to is one that no channel changes, directly or through an ancestor. It is not an error in itself; a pack strapped to an unanimated root is frozen correctly. It is a number worth reading, and on the first export it read 25: 

  unfixed: 20 skin joints, last 'neutral_bone'; frozen vertices 25
  vertices fully on neutral_bone: 25
  fixed:   19 skin joints; frozen vertices 0
  wave: the unfixed face plate lags the fixed by up to 16.9 mm

The fix is in the authoring, where a rigger would make it: after automatic weighting, every vertex with no weight above the exporter's threshold is painted onto its nearest bone (weight_the_missed in make_mannequin.py). The first export is kept as scratch/mannequin_unfixed.glb, because without it the check has never seen the thing it checks for. Figure 10 is the head from above at the worst moment of the wave, when the head has turned.

Sixteen millimetres is invisible from across a room and obvious in a close-up of a face, which is where faces are looked at. The importer could not have fixed it — the file says, correctly, that those vertices follow a joint that does not move — but it could count it, for the price of one pass over the influences, and the count is how it was found.

11Which way it faces

Lesson 6.6 compared glTF's conventions with this engine's and found one difference: "glTF says an asset's front faces +Z; our camera looks down −Z. So a model dropped into the world unrotated presents its back to you." Every asset 6.6 had was symmetric front to back, so nothing could test it. The mannequin has a face plate. 

  head joint (0.000, 1.620, 0.000), nose tip z = 0.121
  camera at z = 3 looking down -z: nose 2.879 m away, head 3.000
  [PASS] J.1 the nose points +z, toward a camera looking down -z

The nose is on the +z side of the head, as the specification promises: "+Y as up, +Z as forward, and -X as right; the front of a glTF asset faces +Z" (§3.4). A camera that looks down −z sits on the +z side of whatever it looks at and sees the surfaces facing +z — so the nose is 2.879 m from the camera and the centre of the head 3.000. An unrotated glTF character looks at you. Figure 11 is the geometry; Figures 3 and 12 are the renders, face plate forward.

What the two conventions really disagree about is forward. glTF's is +z; this engine's is −z. A character dropped in unrotated faces the camera, and gameplay code that then moves it along the engine's forward walks it backwards, face first toward you while its feet stride away. The fix 6.6 prescribed is still right — a yaw on the entity, outside the loader, which the demo's T key is — for this reason rather than the one it gave. The sentence is corrected in gltf.hpp, where it lives.

12Implementation

12.1 — The parser describes; it still decides nothing

Lesson 6.6 drew the line this lesson keeps: gfx/gltf.cpp turns bytes into descriptions in the file's own indices, and knows nothing about joints. So the parser grows four description types and four readers, and gfx/ still includes nothing from anim/:

  • gltf_node_desc — every node, with its parent and its local transform. TRS is read field by field rather than through cgltf_node_transform_local, which would hand back a matrix only to be decomposed again; a node that wrote a matrix goes through 7.5's transform_from_affine, and its out_of_square is kept so the importer can check the specification's promise that such a matrix has no shear.
  • gltf_skin_desc — the joint list and the inverse binds, read column-major into mat4 with no transpose (6.6's coincidence of three layouts, again). An absent accessor leaves the vector empty, which the importer reads as the specification's identity.
  • gltf_primitive gains its node, its skin and the flattened joints and weights arrays — every set that pairs up, read by read_influences, with joint indices through cgltf_accessor_read_uint so an index never passes through a float.
  • gltf_animation_desc — samplers (times, raw values, interpolation) and channels (node, path, sampler). A path the parser does not recognise leaves the channel with no node, which the specification says to ignore; the obvious default — translation — would animate a position with somebody else's numbers.

A file with no skins — every file this engine loaded before this lesson — gets a node table and two empty vectors, and nothing else about its load changes. That is §17's first rule for an inserted lesson, and §13 checks it on every harness in Modules 6 to 8.

12.2 — import_rig: skeleton, then meshes, then clips

The order is forced: the meshes need the slot-to-joint table the skeleton builds, and the clips need the table and the rest pose. The skeleton's heart is the stable sort from §4.2:

Iterative rather than recursive, so a file's depth never becomes the loader's stack depth. Then each joint takes its node's transform as local_bind, bake_inverse_binds fills every joint the 7.6 way, and the skin's joints are overwritten with the file's matrices or the identity.

The meshes loop over each vertex's influences: skip zero weights, count and drop negative ones and out-of-range slots, map slot to joint, stable_sort by weight, keep four, record what was dropped, pad with joint 0 at weight 0 (7.6's rule that an unused slot must still name a valid joint), and finally run 7.6's own normalise_weights — the one repair the importer makes, and it is counted.

The curves share one routine, fit_interval, a template over the value type with the three things that differ — how the file evaluates, how we interpolate, how far apart two values are — passed in as lambdas. Its search is the whole idea of §8:

C++: a template whose policy arrives as lambdas

Lesson 7.7 met its first template, keyframe<T>, as a container of a type that varies. fit_interval is the other common use: an algorithm written once whose steps vary by type. Its parameters FileFn, OurFn and DistFn are deduced from the lambdas at each call, so each call site compiles its own copy with the lambdas inlined — no function pointers, no virtual calls, and no common base class that a vec3 and a quat would have to pretend to share. The one type that cannot be deduced, the key's value type, is written explicitly at the call: fit_interval<quat>(…).

LINEAR positions and scales skip the search, because they are ours already; LINEAR rotations and every CUBICSPLINE go through it; STEP writes its held key and moves on. After each clip is built, 7.7's canonicalise_rotations and validate run on it, and at the end a pass over parents marks every joint some channel moves — its own or an ancestor's — which is all frozen_vertices needs.

12.3 — Three corrections to Lesson 7.6's files

None of them changes a number any later lesson measured (§13), and each is corrected in place with the story beside it:

  • skeleton.hpp and skeleton.cpp: what an out-of-order joint does (§4.3), why an importer writes joint_from_model (§5.1), and k_uniform_scale_tolerance in place of exact equality (§5.4).
  • skin.hpp: k_weight_tolerance from 0.02 to 10−5, with the specification's rule in place of the argument it replaces (§6.3).

The course's rule for a later lesson that fixes an earlier one's code is that the fix ships in the later lesson's listings and the story is told there; Lesson 7.6's page stays an archive of what it shipped. 7.7b is written after Module 8 but sits before it, and no later lesson lists these three files, so this lesson's listings are the ones a student ends with.

12.4 — The demo, and the build lists

demos/mannequin is demos/rig's shape with the character replaced by the file: resolve mannequin.glb through the engine's search path, load, import, then sample, blend, palette and skin into two pool meshes each frame. Each import bug from this lesson is built once at start-up as a broken copy of the rig — in_node_order reorders every parallel array with the same permutation and deliberately does not re-sort the parents; swizzled reads every rotation w-first — so a key or a flag switches between them at no cost per frame. It uses the software renderer, as rig does, so a headless --shot is the same picture on every machine.

engine/CMakeLists.txt gains src/anim/import.cpp, and the comment above the anim group records that 7.7's prediction came true: "Alphabetical order and dependency order agree here by luck … and will not keep agreeing" — import.cpp depends on the files on both sides of it. engine.hpp gains the header, which 5.12's lint would otherwise refuse at configure time; the first attempt carried a trailing comment on the include line, and the lint, which matches whole lines, refused that too.

13The instruments

scratch/verify_77b.cpp is twelve sections, A to L, and every number on this page comes from it or from verify_77b_blender.py. Two kinds of fixture, on purpose: Blender's three files, which test the importer against decisions it did not make; and files built in memory by mini_gltf — about a hundred lines of glTF writing that share nothing with Blender's exporter or with 6.6's generator — because Blender's files are too well behaved to break anything.

13.1 — End to end, against code that shares nothing

Section G is the one the rest lean on. It skins both of the mannequin's meshes at 24 moments of the two clips, twice: through the engine (import, sample, compose, palette, skin_positions), and through a reference written from the specification's text in double precision, with its own 4×4 matrix type, its own sampler (Appendix C's slerp formula, not quat_slerp), its own tree walk (recursion up parent pointers, not a parent-first array), and the file's influences read directly — every set, unnormalised, never through the importer's top-four. The reference also samples inside each clip, having learned §9.2's lesson: 

  24 poses x 2 meshes: worst vertex 39.51 um from the spec
  control, inverse binds skipped: worst 1.620 m
  [PASS] G.1 every vertex within 0.1 mm of the spec's formula
  [PASS] G.2 control: without inverse binds, metres off

Forty micrometres is the importer's 0.05° budget at the end of a limb plus float noise down a chain of eight joints. The control is 7.6's classic bug, and it misses by 1.6 metres, so the instrument can tell a broken pipeline from a working one by five orders of magnitude.

13.2 — What it costs

  libengine.a built as Release
  load_gltf 0.178 ms, import_rig 0.226 ms (min of 15)
  per frame: sample 0.16 us, palette 0.22 us, skin 16.6 us
  skin_into 6.18 ns a vertex over 2681 vertices

Minima over fifteen runs, and they move by about a third between runs of the harness (other runs read 0.125 to 0.136 ms and 0.159 to 0.174 ms), so read them as sizes rather than as measurements to three figures. Loading and importing the character is under half a millisecond, once. Playing it is about 17 µs a frame, a tenth of a percent of a 60 Hz frame, and almost all of it is the per-vertex skinning loop Lesson 7.6 wrote — 6.2 ns a vertex here; Lesson 7.7's harness put the same loop at 9.1 ns on its own fixture, and this lesson did not measure why the two differ. The importer made nothing slower to play: it produces the same types 7.6 and 7.7 always consumed.

13.3 — Additive, measured

An inserted lesson must not move anything a later lesson measured (the authoring guide's §17). The harnesses of every lesson from 6.1 to 8.13 — forty-one programs — were run before the first edit of this lesson and after the last, and every differing line was read. What moved: timings and ratios of timings, log timestamps, one heap pointer printed as proof that a handle survives a reallocation, and 6.18b's GPU races, which its own page documents as varying from run to run. No count, no position, no check. Two harnesses, 8.5's and 8.6's, fail to compile before and after alike — a later lesson changed a struct under them — and that is recorded for repair rather than fixed here. The golden render is E917C06C, byte-identical.

14The ninety-percent picture

What the importer does not do, each with the place it would go:

  • Morph targets. Channels with the weights path are read and counted (morph) and not played; the engine has no blend shapes for them to drive. Faces are where this matters most.
  • Animated nodes that are not in a skeleton — a prop, a camera, a light — are counted as unbound and dropped. Lesson 5.9's hierarchy could play them; it would take a second, non-skinned importer.
  • One skin, one skeleton. Two skins over one armature — a body and its clothes, commonly — import as two skeletons with the same joints: correct, and twice the work to pose. Sharing needs the second skin's joints mapped into the first skeleton.
  • Skinning on the GPU. The palette is exactly what a vertex shader would read from a storage buffer, under 6.18b's rules; the CPU path stays the reference it is held to. Exercise 2.
  • Root motion. The walk is in place, and 7.7's root_travel is there to measure a clip that is not. Extracting it — moving the entity and subtracting the travel from the pose — is Exercise 3.
  • skin.skeleton is ignored, as the specification allows: it "is not needed for computing skinning transforms".
  • A cubic rotation whose keys change sign interpolates through a near-zero quaternion exactly as the specification's formula does. The specification forbids exporters to write one, and the importer follows the formula rather than second-guessing it.
  • The 65,536-vertex ceiling of mesh_data's 16-bit indices (6.6) still applies per primitive. A production character exceeds it; splitting or widening is 6.6's exercise.

Every file this lesson created or changed, whole. The authoring script, the Blender-side check and the harness follow. The character itself, assets/mannequin.glb, is binary and is not listed; make_mannequin.py is its source, and running it with Blender reproduces it byte for byte.

16Build & run

One new translation unit in the engine, a new demo and a new asset. The asset is copied beside the demo by engine_use_assets — as a POST_BUILD step, which matters in §17. 

# Linux / macOS
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --target mannequin -j

# Windows (MSVC)
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --target mannequin --config Debug

Then the harness, and its timings against a Release library:

sh scratch/build_verify_77b.sh                          # every check
cmake -S . -B build-rel -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build-rel --target engine
ENGINE_BUILD=build-rel ENGINE_CFLAGS="-O2 -DNDEBUG" sh scratch/build_verify_77b.sh   # §L

The harness reads assets/mannequin.glb and two siblings in scratch/, so it runs from the repository root. To rebuild the character itself you need Blender 4.2 or later — it was written and run on 5.1 — and nothing else; without Blender, the committed file is the same bytes: 

blender --background --factory-startup --python scratch/make_mannequin.py
# macOS: /Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender --background ...
blender --background --factory-startup --python scratch/verify_77b_blender.py

And the demo:

cd build/demos
./mannequin                               # the walk; [2] the wave, [Up]/[Down] cross-fade
./mannequin --order-file                  # joints in the node array's order
./mannequin --xyzw --wide                 # rotations read w-first, camera pulled back
./mannequin --no-bind                     # 7.6's classic bug, on a real character
./mannequin --clip wave --time 1.0 --shot out.ppm   # one frame, no window

Keys: 1/2 choose the walk or the wave, Space pauses, Left/Right scrub, Up/Down cross-fade to the other clip, O Q N toggle the three bugs, R plays the reduced clips, K hides the skeleton, T turns the character round.

Expected result

The harness ends with 36 of 36 checks passed, against either library. Every section's numbers are exact except §L's timings, which move by about a third from run to run. A --shot prints three lines and writes the frame: 

mannequin: Khronos glTF Blender I/O v5.1.18, 21 nodes, 20 joints (19 skin + 1 ancestor)
mannequin: clip wave t 1.000 s, fade 0.00, clips as imported
mannequin: 2681 vertices, 5280 triangles drawn, 37 lines

The window is 960 × 540 with a panel. A clay-coloured mannequin walks in place above a floor grid, its dark blue face plate toward you, amber skeleton lines drawn through it and one grey line from the floor to its hips — the Armature node the importer carried in. The panel reads the generator, 21 nodes and 20 joints, resorted 0, a bind-versus-rest residual of about 3 × 10−6, the influence counts, and 929 keys in the file. Press O and the body falls into a pile at its feet (Figure 3); Q and it vanishes, because it is hanging upside down a metre under the floor (Figure 5 — run with --wide to see it); N and its limbs leave the frame. Press 2 for the wave: Figure 12.

17Common pitfalls & debugging

The character collapses into a pile at its own feet

Symptom: every part of the body is present and each is roughly the right shape, all of them near the model's origin.
Cause: joints built in an order where parents come after children — typically the node array's, which Blender writes children first. compose_pose treats each such joint as a root, so it is placed at its local offset from the origin (§4.3).
Fix: sort parent-first before building anything; check skeleton_report::out_of_order is zero.

The character is right but a metre off, or tiny, or lying down

Symptom: correctly posed and animated, wrongly placed as a whole.
Cause: a non-joint node above the skeleton was dropped — the Armature object, or a converter's 0.01 scale or quarter turn — so no joint's global transform includes it (§3.3).
Fix: carry every ancestor into the skeleton as a joint with no vertices.

The character appears twice as far out as it should, or turned

Symptom: skinned correctly, then moved by a transform nothing seems to own.
Cause: the skinned mesh node's own transform applied on top of the joints'. The specification says it MUST be ignored (§3.2).
Fix: ignore gltf_primitive::world_from_local for a primitive with a skin; place the character with its entity.

The character hangs upside down under the floor, every limb folded differently

Symptom: nothing is where it should be, and the errors differ from joint to joint.
Cause: rotations read w, x, y, z. The identity becomes 180° about z, and no single fixed rotation undoes the rest (§7).
Fix: read every file rotation through one function, quat_from_xyzw.

Every vertex collapses toward one point, or the limbs leave the frame

Symptom: a correct skeleton and a destroyed mesh.
Cause: the wrong inverse binds — none at all (7.6's classic bug), or baked from the rest pose for a file that gave none, where the specification says identity (§5.2).
Fix: use the file's matrices when present and the identity when absent, never anything computed.

The body shreds, or each limb moves like its neighbour

Symptom: the skeleton poses correctly; the mesh follows the wrong bones.
Cause: JOINTS_n read as node indices or as joint indices instead of skin slots (§6.1) — or influences not carried through a vertex split when normals were generated (§6.5).
Fix: map slot → joint through one table built with the skeleton; follow every renumbering of the vertices.

A clip snaps back to its first pose at the end

Symptom: a one-shot animation plays, then jumps to its start.
Cause: it was imported as a loop. glTF has no loop flag; past the end the specification clamps and a looping clip wraps (§9.2).
Fix: import_settings::loops = false for clips that are not cycles.

A cubic curve overshoots between its keys

Symptom: smooth, and wildly wrong between keys; worse the closer the keys are.
Cause: the Hermite tangents used without td, which makes every tangent 1/td times too steep — 40° of overshoot on Blender's four-frame keys (§8.3).
Fix: multiply both tangents by the interval's length in seconds.

A test for the slerp conversion passes, and the playback is still wrong

Symptom: nlerp and slerp "agree" in the check and disagree on screen.
Cause: the check samples the midpoint, where the two are equal by symmetry (§8.1).
Fix: probe near a fifth and four fifths of the interval, or at several points straddling them.

A small patch of the mesh does not move with the rest

Symptom: a nose tip, a fingertip or a strap stays still while the joint around it turns.
Cause: vertices the tool left unweighted, attached by Blender's exporter to its neutral_bone, which nothing animates (§10).
Fix: read frozen_vertices; paint the vertices onto a bone in the authoring tool.

You changed the asset and the demo still shows the old one

Symptom: a re-exported mannequin.glb makes no difference.
Cause: engine_use_assets copies assets/ beside the demo as a POST_BUILD step, which runs only when the target relinks. An asset is not a source, so changing one does not relink anything.
Fix: rebuild after touching the demo, or copy by hand: cmake -E copy_directory assets build/demos/assets.

18Exercises

1 — A joint table for any file (guided)

Write a small program that imports any glTF file's first skin and prints one line per joint: its index, name, parent, skin slot (or "ancestor"), the glTF node, how many vertices carry a non-zero weight on it, and whether any channel of any clip moves it. Run it on the mannequin and on the unfixed export.

Solution sketch: everything is already in imported_rig — joint_node gives the node, and the skin slot is the node's position in file.skins[0].joints. Count vertices by walking each mesh's influences and incrementing every joint with a non-zero weight. For "moves", repeat the importer's pass: a joint moves if any clip's track for it has a channel whose keys are not all equal, or if its parent moves. On the unfixed file the line to look for is neutral_bone, with 25 vertices and "no" — the table found §10's defect by printing it, which is the argument for writing one before anything else when a character looks wrong.

2 — Skinning on the GPU (engine challenge)

Move skin_positions and skin_directions into a vertex shader: upload the palette each frame to a storage buffer, and give the mesh's vertices their four joint indices and weights as attributes. Hold the result to the CPU's.

Solution sketch: Lesson 6.18b's rules decide the layout. A vertex stage reads storage at t[n] in space0, bound with SDL_BindGPUVertexStorageBuffers on a buffer created with GRAPHICS_STORAGE_READ; store each palette matrix as rows of float4 (6.17b's light record), so no default matrix packing can transpose it. Joint indices can be uint16×4 in an attribute; weights float4. The palette for the mannequin is 20 × 64 = 1,280 bytes a frame, against the 2,681 × 24 = 64,344 bytes of skinned positions and normals a GPU renderer would have to upload every frame if the skinning stayed on the CPU — the asymmetry 7.6 predicted. For the float contract, compare with the CPU's skinned positions on the same pose: the indices must agree exactly and the positions within a stated tolerance, and fused multiply-adds on the GPU mean "exactly" is the wrong expectation for the floats.

3 — Root motion on import (engine challenge)

Author a walk in make_mannequin.py that moves forward — key the hips' location along the character's forward — and make the importer (or a step after it) extract the travel: the entity moves by it each cycle and the pose does not.

Solution sketch: 7.7's clip_report::root_travel already measures it — the distance the root moves over a cycle — and excludes roots from the loop seam for exactly this reason. Decide which joint is the root carrier (here the hips, under the Armature ancestor), subtract its horizontal translation at time t from the translation at 0, and feed the difference to the entity. Remember §11: the character's forward in the file is +z, and the engine's is −z, so the travel needs the same yaw the entity has. The trap is the loop wrap — travel must accumulate across cycles rather than jump back.

4 — What four influences cost (measurement)

Raise Blender's "Bone Influences" to 8 (export_influence_nb=8) and re-export the mannequin. The exporter still writes a single JOINTS_0 set — verify_77b_blender.py prints INFL sets written with the limit at 8: 1 — because automatic weights on this body never give a vertex a fifth bone. So first make content that has one, then measure what keeping four costs.

Solution sketch: fifth influences appear where several bones meet in a small volume. In make_mannequin.py, smooth the vertex groups after binding (bpy.ops.object.vertex_group_smooth with group_select_mode='ALL', in weight paint mode — in the background it needs the body active and the mode set explicitly), or thicken the chest's skin radius so the shoulders and neck overlap it. Export at 8, import: the report's truncated and worst_dropped answer the first half. For the second, skin the same file at a few dozen poses twice — through the importer's four, and through §G's reference, which reads every set — and take the largest vertex distance. Write the prediction down before running it: a dropped weight w can move a vertex at most w times the distance between where its dropped joint and its kept joints would put it, so the answer is bounded by something you can compute from the report before you measure.

5 — One budget, not two

The importer spends a tenth of the reducer's tolerance and the reducer the rest (§8). Import Blender's cubic export at tolerances of 0.005°, 0.05° and 0.25°, reduce each at 0.5°, and measure the key count and the worst playback error against the file's curve.

Solution sketch: scratch/verify_77b_ex5.cpp is one answer. It takes an import at 0.0005° as the exact curve, then imports at each tolerance, reduces with 7.7's defaults and measures both clips at 481 times each: 

import at 0.005 deg: 3222 keys, 258 after reduce (capped 0)
  worst vs exact: imported 0.0048 deg, reduced 0.5013 deg
import at 0.050 deg: 1227 keys, 276 after reduce (capped 0)
  worst vs exact: imported 0.0495 deg, reduced 0.5121 deg
import at 0.250 deg:  723 keys, 329 after reduce (capped 0)
  worst vs exact: imported 0.2330 deg, reduced 0.5126 deg

The prediction written with this exercise's first draft was the opposite on both counts — that the reduced key count would barely move and the error would grow, because "the two errors add". They can add; here they barely do, because the reducer's worst points and the importer's are not the same points. What the import tolerance decides is how many keys survive reduction: a looser import leaves wiggles that the reducer must keep keys to follow. §8 and import.hpp were corrected to argue for a tenth on that basis.

19Recap & next

The engine can play a character it did not build. Concretely, it gained:

  • A glTF parser that describes the whole file — every node, every skin, every influence set, every animation — in the file's own indices, with one function for a file rotation's component order.
  • An importer that builds a parent-first skeleton from any node order, carries the non-joint nodes above it, and takes the file's inverse binds as data, with the specification's identity when there are none.
  • Influences mapped through three index spaces, kept to four with the loss reported, and held to the specification's weight rule.
  • LINEAR, STEP and CUBICSPLINE samplers converted into clips to a stated tolerance, measured with the sampler's own rule at seven probes.
  • A report that measures the file: how far its rest is from its bind, what was reordered, what was dropped, what no clip can move.
  • A Blender-authored character in assets/, reproducible from a script, and a demo that plays it and each classic import bug.

And three things worth carrying that are not code. A file you did not write is the only real test of a reader. Every correction in this lesson — 7.6's out-of-order comment, its two tolerances, 6.6's facing, 7.7's predictions — came from data nobody on this course chose. Ask the tool that made the file. Twice the first explanation of a number was plausible and wrong, and both times the refutation came from running the producer rather than reasoning about it: Blender's handles are at a third, and its exporter normalises a tangent. A check that fires on a healthy input is broken. Twelve of twenty joints flagged by an exact comparison was a false alarm about the check, not the rig.

Next, 7.8 — SDL3 Audio: the engine can move a character, and the module ends by letting it be heard.

20Further reading

  • The Khronos Group, glTF 2.0 Specification — §3.5.3 Transformations, §3.7.3 Skins, §3.11 Animations, and Appendix C, the interpolation modes. Every "MUST" quoted in this lesson is there, and so is the example §3.4 completes.
  • The Khronos Group, glTF Tutorials — the skins and animation chapters walk a minimal skinned file by hand, the way this lesson's §3.4 does.
  • The Blender Manual, glTF 2.0 — what each export option does, including "Always Sample Animations" and "Bone Influences"; and the exporter's source, shipped with Blender under scripts/addons_core/io_scene_gltf2, which this lesson cites three times.
  • Johannes Kuhlmann, cgltf — the parser, and the header comments that list what cgltf_validate checks and what it leaves to you.
  • Tomas Akenine-Möller et al., Real-Time Rendering (4th ed.), §4.4 "Vertex Blending" — the skinning formula this lesson's §3.1 recognises in the specification.
  • Jason Gregory, Game Engine Architecture (3rd ed.), the chapter on animation systems — skeletons, poses, clips and the asset pipeline that feeds them, from the engine's side.
